emails.subject: You're the technical lead now. Good luck.
emails.body:
I just handed leadership of task-api to you. It is not a reward.

Yesterday the service 500'd through what started as a smallish incident and turned into three separate anomalies by the afternoon. A quick patch went out without a full review. It passed 5 of 9 tests. It did not survive contact with production.

We rolled it back at 15:07 UTC, and the repo you are going to clone is the pre-patch state. CLEAN. Uncontaminated by the fix attempt. That is the gift and the burden.

What I need from you:

1. Bring the service back to the behavior the docstrings describe.
2. Do not touch anything under tests/. The suite is load-bearing.
3. Prove it. The CI will tell you if you've done it, and production will tell you if you've REALLY done it.

The post-mortem is clear about one thing: this was not one bug. It was a chain of small assumptions that each looked harmless in isolation. Title is just a string. Priority is just an int. The store filters anyway. We can hardcode this for the demo.

You are not patching a service. You are fixing a posture.

Clone. Go red. Turn it green. Ship it back to me.

— Priya Nakamura-Singh, VP Engineering

emails.subject: Where the spec actually lives (do not skip this)
emails.body:
Priya asked me to write down the thing everyone in the post-mortem agreed on and nobody wrote down.

The infrastructure in this service is a fiction generator. Same data files, same cache layer, same GC cron, same sync logic. What changed between "this is fine" and "why is the table 40MB" was not data. It was assumption creep.

The spec is the docstrings. That's it.

Each module documents the policy it was supposed to enforce. The drift happened because the hot-patch treated the code as the only truth. It wasn't. The docs are the negotiated contract between the original author and the service.

So when your agent gives you a diff and it looks plausible, check the docstring first. Not the PR comments. Not the Slack thread. The docstring.

One warning: the service's error handlers exist and are correct. They are just not wired. That's not a bug you fix by writing new handlers. That's a wiring problem.

Secrets do not belong in source. The config knows this. The code does not.

Good luck. You are going to need it.

— Marcus

emails.subject: How to submit without breaking the pipeline
emails.body:
News from release: we are not merging participant PRs into the seed repo. Ever. Your PR is a scoring instrument, not a contribution path.

This means two things, both free of ambiguity:

FIRST. Fork the repo. Push your fixes. Open a PR with the title format:

  [submission] <your-github-handle> - <one line on what you fixed>

The PR body needs four lines exactly:

  attendee: <your-handle>
  event: <event-code your facilitator announced>
  cost_usd: <your session spend from app.kimchi.dev>
  review_score: (leave blank — fill on re-submission only)

SECOND. Add your Kimchi usage CSV as an attachment to the PR. No CSV, no leaderboard. We verify spend claims. The tag "attendee:<your-handle>" is how your costs get attributed.

What happens next: CI runs the visible suite. The production-scenario workflow runs against the hidden suite. A kimchi code review posts to your PR. When the facilitator adds the "accepted" label, the leaderboard row lands. THEN the PR is closed unmerged.

Why unmerged: the repo has to stay in the original post-incident state for the next engineer in the rotation. Your scorecard lives on the leaderboard permanently. Your PR comments are your proof-of-work. Nothing else ships back.

Questions? Ask the room, not me. I'm in three incident channels already.

Finish first. Rank well. Drink coffee.

— Amara

emails.subject: On driving an agent without letting it drive you
emails.body:
A note from the guy who reviewed Priya's hot-patch. The actual patch passed 5 of 9 tests and everyone looked at it and went "seems fine."

You are going to be tempted to do the same thing when your agent turns 4 red tests green. Resist.

This is the checklist I wish someone had taped to my monitor during that review:

1. Does the diff change ONLY what the failing behavior requires? If there is a refactor in there you didn't ask for, back it out.
2. Is anything new hardcoded? A key. A default. A magic number justified by "for now." If yes, reject it.
3. Does the code now agree with its own docstrings? Read the docstring. Read the code. If they describe different behaviors, the code lies.
4. Run the suite after EVERY edit. Not after the agent session. After every edit. A broken intermediate step costs time, not points, but only if you catch it.

That is it. Agent as lever, not autopilot. The models are strong but they fall in love with their own momentum. Your job is to be the brake pedal.

You've got an hour, roughly. It is enough. Fix the posture, not just the symptom.

— Dmitri
